newsitem.title: ITALY: Hollywood diva Bacall stars in Rome couture show.
newsitem.headline: Hollywood diva Bacall stars in Rome couture show.

text.p: Even at 72, Lauren Bacall still gets stage fright. Especially when she's starring in a brand new role as a catwalk model.

The Hollywood diva made her debut on the runway for Italian designer Gai Mattiolo on Sunday night as he turned ancient Rome's Capitol Hill into a Venetian canalside for his autumn-winter 1997-98 "alta moda" (haute couture) collection.
For the woman who once said she was nicknamed "The Look" because she trembled from nerves so badly she had to keep her chin down and look through her lashes, some things never change.
"It was like an opening night," Humphrey Bogart's leading lady on- and off-screen told Reuters after the show. "I was nerve-racked."
Mattiolo's models, their hair coiffed and ringletted like eighteenth century aristocrats, sashayed down a runway past brightly-painted gondolas with a fountain trickling behind them.
The 28-year-old Roman designer, who said he picked Venice as his theme because of its harmonious blend of styles and traditions, composed a theatrical collection in rich hues.
There were slim sheath dresses incorporating the Venetian mask motif in tailoring at the back or printed on the fabric.
Harlequin-patterned outfits came in pastels or reds and oranges while fairy-tale tutus and puffball skirts went with tights printed with roses and with a golden seam.
Broad Marie Antoinette-style frocks cheekily incorporated silk panels printed with cherubs and copies of Old Masters such as Canaletto and Titian with skirts of peacock and gold.
One gorgeous ivory gown came trimmed with tiny pink roses and ribbons and a frothy, sweeping train.

Silhouette was all -- from the military-inspired black brocade jackets with gold or cream embroidery, sleek cream pants and knee-high black stiletto boots that opened the show to the narrow floor-length coats with huge feather boa-like collars.
Suits were nifty, with trim decollete jackets that flared over the hip paired with tiny mini-skirts and perilous heels.
Slinky dresses fanned out behind to give a curvy, feminine, mermaid-like shape, or else were pared down to figure-hugging forms with bold slits not for the coy.
One metallic-looking gold bustier bared a breast and its long black skirt was cropped to the minimum at the front.
Sequins spangled in one bright jacket with a scene of Venice over fluid powder-blue pants. Silver briefs stood out under a black lace dress and silver bodices shone over scarlet skirts.
There were sleek dresses of twinkling white that turned gradually into sparkly black as if dipped into ink.
Materials came in fine velvets, brocades and lace -- some floral and in flounces, some sheer and sexy.

While the lights projected an image of Venice's fire-gutted Fenice opera house on the palace behind the elegant square designed by Michelangelo, one model whirled out in a scarlet headdress and red sequin flames licking round a slim gold dress.

But the blonde Bacall stole the show at the end with a simple, sleek long-sleeved black dress with keyhole neck at the front. Over her shoulder she draped an embroidered stole that kept slipping off, but she stayed cool, smiling and waving.
"I enjoyed it, it was so lovely," she said in her famously husky tones. But asked if she foresaw the start of a new career, she burst out laughing. "I don't think so," she said.
Rome's fashion shows climax with a star-studded gala on the Spanish Steps on Wednesday.
